```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 7,
  fig.height = 5
)
library(multinma)
library(mid.nma.rank)
options(mc.cores = 2)
```

## Introduction

This vignette shows how to rank treatments in a standard network
meta-analysis (NMA) while requiring a minimally important difference
(MID) when ranking treatments. The approach follows an example illustration from Curteis et al. (2025).[@curteis2025ranking]

The example uses the `Senn2013` diabetes data supplied with **multinma**
which was originally sourced from Senn et al. (2013)[@senn2013issues] The dataset consists of 26
studies on 10 treatments (including placebo), and the outcome under
consideration is the mean difference in change from baseline in mean
HbA1c, a measure of blood sugar attached to haemoglobin and an indicator
of average blood sugar levels in preceding weeks.

## Data and network

Each row displays mean differences (y) and associated standard errors (se) in HbA1c for a treatment (trt) compared to a reference treatment in each study (study).

```{r data}
data(Senn2013)
head(Senn2013)
```

One reference arm in Study Willms 1999 has a missing standard error, which for the purposes of this example we naively impute with a value of 0.4.

```{r impute}
Senn2013$se[Senn2013$study == "Willms1999"][2] <- 0.4
```

The network diagram is shown below, with many connections via placebo, and multiple loops within the network.

```{r network}
diabetes_net <- set_agd_contrast(
  Senn2013,
  study = study,
  trt = trt,
  y = y,
  se = se,
  trt_ref = "Placebo"
)
plot(diabetes_net)
```

## Fit the model

Due to the number of studies informing each treatment contrast, the random effects model was preferred over the fixed effects model.

```{r fit, results = "hide", message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
diabetes_fit_RE <- nma(diabetes_net,
                       trt_effects = "random",
                       prior_intercept = normal(scale = 1000),
                       prior_trt = normal(scale = 1000),
                       iter = 2000,  
                       chains = 4)
```

```{r fit-summary}
diabetes_fit_RE
```

## Choosing the Minimally Important Difference (MID)

The MID must be on the same scale as the model's treatment effects. Here
the effects are mean differences in HbA1c (percentage points), so we
require a difference of at least certain difference of percentage points before one treatment is ranked above another. 

A difference between groups of 0.3 in % HbA1c is considered to be clinically meaningful for patients with type 2 diabetes[@ewers2024effects; @schwingshackl2018network;  @look2010long], so we take 0.3 as the MID in this example. 

Importantly, this differs from a minimally important change (MIC; defined as the smallest within-patient change in an outcome measure that is considered important by patients or clinicians) value of 0.5% reported in the literature, which was not used here.

```{r mid}
mid <- 0.3
```

It is important to pre-specify the MID and for it to be well motivated by available literature.

## Rankings without an MID

For comparison, treatment rankings without incorporation of an MID are displayed below. In particular, the plot below displays the posterior median ranks of each treatment along with 50% and 97.5% credible intervals.

```{r rank-standard}
rank_0 <- posterior_ranks(diabetes_fit_RE, sucra = TRUE)
plot(rank_0)
```

## Rankings with an MID

We then generate the posterior median ranks of each treatment, accounting for a difference of 0.3 in HbA1c as the MID. Also available are the MID-adjusted mean ranks and MID-adjusted SUCRAs.

```{r rank-mid}
rank_mid <- posterior_ranks_mid(
  diabetes_fit_RE,
  summary = TRUE,
  sucra = TRUE,
  mid = mid
)
rank_mid
```

```{r rank-mid-plot}
plot(rank_mid)
```

### Rank probabilities

We can also generate the posterior rank probabilities for each treatment, which are the probabilities of each treatment being ranked first, second, third, etc. The plot below shows the rank probabilities for each treatment accounting for the MID. Note that with an MID, it is possible for their to be ties between treatments. In Curteis et al. (2025), the authors recommend using the "midpoint" method for handling ties, which is the default in `posterior_rank_probs_mid()`.[@curteis2025ranking] We therefore see treatments having positive probabilities of being placed in a rank of, for example, 1.5, which is not possible without an MID.

```{r rank-probs}
rank_probs <- posterior_rank_probs(diabetes_fit_RE) #without mid
rank_probs_mid <- posterior_rank_probs_mid(diabetes_fit_RE, mid = mid) #with mid
rank_probs_mid
plot(rank_probs_mid)
```

### Cumulative rank probabilities

The cumulative probability of being ranked in a certain position or better can also be generated, again accounting for an MID.

```{r rank-probs-cum}
rank_probs_cum_mid <- posterior_rank_probs_mid(
  diabetes_fit_RE,
  cumulative = TRUE,
  mid = mid
)
plot(rank_probs_cum_mid)
```


### MID-Adjusted SUCRAs

The purpose of using the "midpoint" method to handling ties is that this retains the desirable property that the average SUCRA value in a network is 0.5. The below table collates median ranks, MID-SUCRAs and P Best with and without an MID. The final column displays the probability of being best or equal best (i.e. within an MID of the best treatment) for each treatment.

```{r rank-table}
# round numbers to specified number of digits
digits <- function(x, dig = 1, adj = 0) {
  sprintf(paste0("%." , dig, "f"), as.numeric(x)+adj)
}

#Estimate the probability of being best or equal best (i.e. within an MID of the best treatment) for each treatment
p_mid_best <- rank_probs_mid$summary$p_best_or_equal

#Generate a table displaying useful ranking information for each treatment, including median rank, SUCRA, and probability of being best (with and without MID)
rank_table <- cbind(rank_0$summary$`50%`,
                    rank_mid$summary$`50%`,
                    digits(rank_0$summary$sucra, 2),
                    digits(rank_mid$summary$sucra, 2),
                    digits(rank_probs$summary$`p_rank[1]`,2),
                    digits(rank_probs_mid$summary$`p_rank[1]`,2),
                    digits(p_mid_best,2))
rank_table <- as.data.frame(rank_table)
colnames(rank_table) <- c("Median Rank", "MID-Median Rank",
                          "SUCRA", "MID-SUCRA",
                          "P Best", "P MID Best", "P MID Equal Best")
rownames(rank_table) <- rank_0$summary$.trt
rank_table
```
